Agentic Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive and Quantum Aware Network Routing
radar.venue: The International journal of networked and distributed computing
radar.venue_raw: The International journal of networked and distributed computing
radar.summary: Efficient and adaptive routing remains a critical challenge in dynamic network environments due to changing traffic conditions, network congestion, and link failures. Traditional routing approaches, such as Dijkstra and OSPF, rely on static or semi-adaptive mechanisms, which limit their ability to respond to real-time network variations. To address these limitations, this paper proposes an Agentic Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (AMARL) framework for intelligent and decentralized routing. In the proposed model, each network node operates as an autonomous agent capable of observing local network conditions, communicating with neighboring agents, and making cooperative routing decisions. A multi-objective reward function is designed to jointly optimize delay, throughput, packet delivery ratio, and packet loss. The framework enables dynamic adaptation to network changes without requiring global recomputation. Extensive simulations are conducted under varying network sizes, traffic conditions, and link failure scenarios. The results demonstrate that the proposed AMARL model achieves significant performance improvements, including up to 45% higher throughput, 35% lower delay, and over 50% reduction in packet loss compared to traditional methods. Furthermore, the model maintains higher reliability under link failures and exhibits fast convergence with reduced energy consumption over training episodes. These findings indicate that the integration of agentic intelligence and multi-agent cooperation provides a scalable, adaptive, and efficient solution for next-generation network routing. The proposed framework is particularly suitable for dynamic and large-scale network environments where traditional routing methods fail to perform effectively.

radar.title: The Virtual Biotech: A multi-agent AI framework for therapeutic discovery and development
radar.summary: Drug development requires evidence integration across biological scales and modalities, but relevant tools are fragmented. We introduce the Virtual Biotech, an organization of artificial intelligence (AI) agents modeled on a drug-development company, with agentic divisions spanning target discovery, safety assessment, modality selection, and clinical development. We demonstrate its utility at three drug-development decision points. First, more than 37,000 agents annotated outcomes from 55,984 trials and found that drugs targeting cell type–specific genes were 48% more likely to reach market with 32% fewer adverse events. Second, it integrated multimodal evidence to propose a therapeutic strategy in lung cancer. Third, it analyzed a terminated ulcerative colitis trial and inferred potential mechanisms of failure. These results demonstrate that human-guided multi-agent systems can conduct transparent, multiscale analyses to inform therapeutic-development decisions.

Strong Nash Equilibria of Core-Selecting Double Auctions
radar.summary: We study core-selecting auctions for double auctions that incorporate package bidding. Unlike in one-sided core-selecting auctions, the core may be empty in more general double auction settings, and truncation strategies need not be amongst a bidder’s best responses. Nevertheless, we establish the existence of a core-selecting auction in which every imputation in the core with respect to true preferences corresponds to a strong Nash equilibrium. Specifically, for any core imputation, there exists a profile of truncation strategies that constitutes a strong Nash equilibrium and induces precisely that imputation.
radar.summary_short: We study core-selecting auctions for double auctions that incorporate package bidding. Unlike in one-sided core-selecting auctions, the core may be empty in more general double auction settings, and truncation strategies need not be amongst a bidder’s best responses.

radar.title: Non-equilibrium resonance scattering in intramolecular charge transport drives conformational changes
radar.summary: Abstract Intramolecular charge transport is conventionally described as proceeding along a static ground-state potential, with the carrier acting as a passive probe of a fixed electronic landscape. Here, using alkanethiolate-based molecular junctions, we show that the carrier itself can drive conformational reorganization once the applied bias brings backbone-delocalized molecular orbitals into the transmission window. Combined electrical and in situ structural measurements resolve a threshold-activated transition to a gauche-defect state coincident with the onset of orbital-mediated transport. We rationalize this coupling through a quantum resonance scattering framework in which accessible orbitals act as scattering potentials that transiently host the injected charge, depositing energy into nuclear motion with an efficiency set by molecule–electrode coupling and Franck–Condon overlap. The framework quantitatively reproduces the measured response and predicts the enhanced behavior of amide-containing junctions. Together, these results suggest that charge-transport–structure feedback can be understood in terms of microscopic parameters governing resonance-mediated energy transfer, and that these parameters may be tuned through chemical design.
radar.summary_short: Abstract Intramolecular charge transport is conventionally described as proceeding along a static ground-state potential, with the carrier acting as a passive probe of a fixed electronic landscape.

radar.title: Supervising the search process produces reliable and generalizable information-seeking agents
radar.summary: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are transforming web search by shifting from document ranking to synthesizing answers, and are increasingly deployed as autonomous agentic search systems that iteratively interact with external knowledge sources. Despite this progress, building effective search agents remains challenging because high-quality intermediate search steps are difficult to generate. Previous approaches have primarily relied on outcome supervision, rewarding agents only for producing correct final answers. This often leads to reward hacking and excessive dependence on parametric memory, limiting generalization to out-of-domain tasks. To address these limitations, we introduce RAG-Gym, a framework that shifts supervision from final answers to the search process itself. With RAG-Gym, we systematically investigate architecture design, parameter optimization, and action evaluation, identifying reasoning reflection as a critical capability for search agents. Building on this insight, we propose Re 2 Search++, a process-supervised agent that achieves substantial improvements on multi-hop information-seeking benchmarks, especially in out-of-domain settings. Performance gains are driven primarily by higher-quality search queries rather than answer optimization alone, and the learned search critics transfer across models, including proprietary LLMs. These findings show that supervising the search process produces more reliable and generalizable information-seeking agents.
radar.summary_short: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are transforming web search by shifting from document ranking to synthesizing answers, and are increasingly deployed as autonomous agentic search systems that iteratively interact with external knowledge sources.

radar.title: Optimal Power Scheduling on Cyber‐Physical Systems Subject to DoS Attacks: A Stackelberg Game Analysis
radar.summary: ABSTRACT This article presents an optimal power scheduling strategy for cyber‐physical systems (CPS) vulnerable to denial‐of‐service (DoS) attacks. Departing from conventional Nash equilibrium approaches, we establish a Stackelberg game framework to model the strategic interactions between a multi‐type defender and a multi‐type attacker under information asymmetry, where both parties possess only probabilistic estimates of each other's total power resources. The work systematically develops optimal defense and attack strategies and proposes a Quantum‐behaved Particle Swarm Optimization (QPSO) algorithm to efficiently solve the resulting nonlinear, non‐convex optimization problem. To validate this method, we evaluated it in terms of rewards and convergence rates. Comprehensive simulation validates the effectiveness and superiority of the proposed approach.

radar.title: Pure-Strategy Equilibrium in the Generalized First-Price Auction
radar.summary: We revisit the classic result on the (non-)existence of pure-strategy Nash equilibria in the generalized first-price auction for sponsored search advertising and show that the conclusion may be reversed when ads are ranked based on the product of stochastic quality scores and bid amounts rather than solely on the bids or on the product of bids and deterministic quality scores. Moreover, the expected revenue in the pure-strategy equilibrium of the generalized first-price auction may substantially exceed that of the generalized second-price auction, although under some conditions, the relation may also be reversed. History: This paper has been accepted for the Mathematics of Operations Research Special Issue on Market Design.

radar.title: Robust Auction Design with Support Information
radar.summary: A seller wants to sell an item to n buyers. Buyer valuations are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) according to a distribution unknown to the seller; the seller only knows that the support is included in [a, b]. To be robust, the seller chooses a dominant strategy incentive compatible mechanism that optimizes the worst-case performance relative to the ideal expected revenue the seller could have collected with knowledge of buyers’ valuations. Our analysis unifies the regret and the ratio objectives. For these objectives, we derive an optimal mechanism and the corresponding performance in quasi-closed form, as a function of the support information [a, b] and the number of buyers n. Our analysis reveals three regimes of support information and a new class of robust mechanisms. (i) When a/b is below a threshold, the optimal mechanism is a second-price auction (SPA) with random reserve, a focal class in earlier literature. (ii) When a/b is above another threshold, SPAs are strictly suboptimal, and an optimal mechanism belongs to a class of mechanisms we introduce, which we call pooling auctions (POOL); whenever the highest value is above a threshold, the mechanism still allocates to the highest bidder, but otherwise the mechanism allocates to a uniformly random buyer, that is, pools low types. (iii) When a/b is between two thresholds, a randomization between SPA and POOL is optimal. We also characterize optimal mechanisms within nested central subclasses of mechanisms: standard mechanisms that only allocate to the highest bidder, SPA with random reserve, and SPA with no reserve. We show strict separations in terms of performance across classes, implying that deviating from standard mechanisms is necessary for robustness. Lastly, we show that the same results hold under other distribution classes that capture “positive dependence,” namely i.i.d., mixture of i.i.d., and exchangeable and affiliated distributions, as well as i.i.d. regular distributions. This paper was accepted by David Simchi-Levi, revenue management and market analytics. Supplemental Material: The online appendices are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.02703 .
radar.summary_short: A seller wants to sell an item to n buyers. Buyer valuations are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) according to a distribution unknown to the seller; the seller only knows that the support is included in [a, b].

radar.title: Reusability report: multi-sample omics network inference operates in distinct robustness regimes defined by prior knowledge and data availability
radar.summary: Abstract Knowledge-constrained network inference enables the reconstruction of regulatory programmes from high-dimensional biological data, yet the conditions under which shared and context-specific structures can be reliably identified remain poorly understood. Pablo Rodriguez-Mier et al. recently introduced CORNETO, a framework for multi-sample constrained inference. Here we reproduce, evaluate and extend CORNETO in terms of robustness, identifiability and bias–variance trade-offs. Using dynamic haematopoiesis and stable cortical datasets, we systematically assess four network reconstruction paradigms while preserving the original method-specific evaluation procedures and benchmark definitions. We show that multi-sample inference generally improves robustness and reproducibility, although gains in predictive performance depend on biological context and the completeness of the prior network. To enhance stability, we introduce bootstrap aggregation and selective re-expansion strategies that improve consensus robustness and recovery while preserving context-specific signals without modifying the underlying optimization scheme or sacrificing generality. Across datasets and methods, our results reveal distinct inference regimes governed by sample availability, prior knowledge and regularization. Together, these findings position network reconstruction as a regime-dependent learning problem and provide practical principles for robust multi-sample biological network inference.
radar.summary_short: Abstract Knowledge-constrained network inference enables the reconstruction of regulatory programmes from high-dimensional biological data, yet the conditions under which shared and context-specific structures can be reliably identified remain poorly understood. A diffusion world model and multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for predictive routing in healthcare IoT
radar.summary: Abstract Healthcare Internet of Things (H-IoT) networks support monitoring through wearable sensors, implantable devices, bedside units, mobile gateways, edge nodes, and cloud platforms. Reliable routing is challenging as medical packets are delay-sensitive, while networks face limited energy, mobility, lossy links, congestion, traffic bursts, and sudden node or link failures. This paper presents a diffusion world model and multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) framework for predictive H-IoT routing. The proposed design models the network as a dynamic graph, uses a Temporal Graph Transformer (TGT) to model spatial-temporal dependencies, forecasts link stability, congestion, and failure risk, and uses decentralized agents to select next hops. In ten paired, pre-configured software-emulation scenarios, the executable routing reference prototype achieved measured mean packet delivery ratio of $$56.24\pm 4.75\%$$ , delay of $$42.79\pm 3.34$$ ms, application goodput of $$6.11\pm 0.51$$ kbps, repair overhead of $$0.151\pm 0.024$$ , sensor-radio energy of $$8.94\pm 0.02$$ J, recovery time of $$0.0297\pm 0.0005$$ s, and restricted mean time to first sensor death of $$272.5\pm 44.9$$ s. Source-informed baseline adaptations achieved higher delivery and goodput and lower delay, while the prototype recovered successful routes faster. A separate 20-seed federated-predictor benchmark on emulated patient-group data reported patient-level DP-SGD accountant bound $$(\epsilon ,\delta )=(8,10^{-5})$$ . DP-FedAvg with rehearsal achieved task-1 and task-2 accuracies of $$72.26\pm 1.06\%$$ and $$70.16\pm 0.94\%$$ , respectively, with $$2.24\pm 0.84$$ percentage points of task-1 forgetting.
radar.summary_short: Abstract Healthcare Internet of Things (H-IoT) networks support monitoring through wearable sensors, implantable devices, bedside units, mobile gateways, edge nodes, and cloud platforms.

radar.title: The Data-Driven Censored Newsvendor Problem
radar.summary: We study a censored variant of the data-driven newsvendor problem, where the decision maker must select an ordering quantity that minimizes expected overage and underage costs based only on offline censored sales data rather than historical demand realizations. Our goal is to understand how the degree of historical demand censoring affects the performance of any learning algorithm for this problem. To isolate this impact, we adopt a distributionally robust optimization framework, evaluating policies according to their worst-case regret over an ambiguity set of distributions. This set is defined by the largest historical order quantity (the observable boundary of the data set), and contains all distributions matching the true demand distribution up to this boundary while allowing them to be arbitrary afterward. We demonstrate a spectrum of achievability under demand censoring by deriving a natural necessary and sufficient condition under which vanishing regret is an achievable goal. In regimes in which it is not, we exactly characterize the information loss due to censoring: an insurmountable lower bound on the performance of any policy, even when the decision maker has access to infinitely many demand samples. We then leverage these sharp characterizations to propose a natural robust algorithm that adapts to the historical level of demand censoring. We derive finite-sample guarantees for this algorithm across all possible censoring regimes and show its near-optimality with matching lower bounds (up to polylogarithmic factors). We moreover demonstrate its robust performance via extensive numerical experiments on both synthetic and real-world data sets. This paper was accepted by Wolfram Wiesemann, data science. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.09021 .
radar.summary_short: We study a censored variant of the data-driven newsvendor problem, where the decision maker must select an ordering quantity that minimizes expected overage and underage costs based only on offline censored sales data rather than historical demand realizations.

radar.title: Cooling fast and slow: Characterizing the effects of vitrification in cryo-EM and the subsequent recovery of equilibrium populations
radar.venue_raw: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
radar.summary: Single-particle cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM), a powerful class of techniques in structural biology with the potential to resolve molecular ensembles, requires that samples be vitrified to protect them from the high vacuum of the electron microscope. However, the effects of vitrification on biomolecular ensembles are unknown. To study them, we carried out extensive molecular dynamics simulations (over 50 ms) of the Trp-cage miniprotein at equilibrium and undergoing rapid cooling. We simulated seven cooling rates spanning three orders of magnitude, with the slowest coolings matching experimental rates. By inspecting molecular mobility and density-temperature trajectories for water with and without protein, we found that water vitrification is unaltered by the protein. To track protein conformation changes, and to relate them to kinetics, we made a Markov State Model (MSM) of Trp-cage from 5.4 ms of equilibrium sampling at 277 K. We observed that MSM states with a characteristic time longer than the duration of the nonequilibrium cooling tend to be more robust to artifacts induced by such cooling. Critically, although we observe that some states vanish in the equilibrium ensemble at 230 K, none do in our nonequilibrium cooled ensembles. To account for these perturbations, we developed a thermodynamic inference framework for recovering equilibrium populations from vitrified ensembles. These results indicate that cryo-EM has the capacity to be an accurate technique for the study of biomolecular ensembles.
radar.summary_short: Single-particle cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM), a powerful class of techniques in structural biology with the potential to resolve molecular ensembles, requires that samples be vitrified to protect them from the high vacuum of the electron microscope.

radar.title: Uniform Value and Decidability in Ergodic Blind Stochastic Games
radar.summary: We study a class of two-player zero-sum stochastic games known as blind stochastic games, where players neither observe the state nor receive any information about it during the game. A central concept for analyzing long-duration stochastic games is the uniform value. A game has a uniform value v if for every [Formula: see text], Player 1 (resp., Player 2) has a strategy such that, for all sufficiently large n, his average payoff over n stages is at least [Formula: see text] (resp., at most [Formula: see text]). Prior work has shown that the uniform value may not exist in general blind stochastic games. To address this, we introduce a subclass called ergodic blind stochastic games, defined by imposing an ergodicity condition on the state transitions. For this subclass, we prove the existence of the uniform value and provide an algorithm to approximate it, establishing the decidability of the approximation problem. Notably, this decidability result is novel even in the single-player setting of Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs). Furthermore, we show that no algorithm can compute the uniform value exactly, emphasizing the tightness of our result. Finally, we establish that the uniform value is independent of the initial belief. radar.summary_short: We study a class of two-player zero-sum stochastic games known as blind stochastic games, where players neither observe the state nor receive any information about it during the game. A central concept for analyzing long-duration stochastic games is the uniform value.

radar.title: Assume/Guarantee Contracts for the Compositional Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning of Heterogeneous Teams
radar.summary: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) problems for heterogeneous teams require agents to collaborate to complete team tasks while making the best use of diverse agent capabilities. We introduce assume/guarantee contracts for heterogeneous multi-agent systems (AGC-MAS) and Iterative Heterogeneous Assignment for MARL (IHA-MARL). AGC-MAS contracts are compositional objects that encode the assumptions provided to, and the guarantees required of, each subtask contributing to the overall team task. We formulate contracts as tuples that specify a subtask, an automaton, timeout and success-probability requirements, and dispatch behavior. The automaton tracks an agent's high-level progress through the subtask associated with its contract and provides a natural mechanism for synchronization across contracts. Our abstraction enables robust interaction across heterogeneous low-level subtask implementations, allows heterogeneous agents to substitute for one another in satisfying contracts, and supports reuse of previously satisfied contracts in new team contexts. Having defined our theoretical framework, we develop a decomposition algorithm that breaks down a team task into a set of contracts. We then propose an iterative algorithm for task assignment and MARL that alternates between assigning contracts representing subtasks to individual agents, training the assigned agents to satisfy their contracts, and assessing their resulting capabilities to inform the next round of task assignments until the team's success probability meets the desired threshold. Our experimental results demonstrate the versatility of contracts in enabling agent substitution and contract reuse. Across three benchmarks with five seeds each, IHA-MARL achieves observed $100\%$ final evaluation success. In CPU timing pilots, comparable baselines required approximately $7$--$11\times$ more training-loop time.
radar.summary_short: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) problems for heterogeneous teams require agents to collaborate to complete team tasks while making the best use of diverse agent capabilities.

radar.title: EduAgent-RL: A Human-Centered Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Framework for Personalized Learning, Adaptive Feedback, and Student Performance Prediction
radar.venue: International Journal of Computer Applications Technology and Research
radar.venue_raw: International Journal of Computer Applications Technology and Research
radar.summary: Personalization in digital learning is often handled through separate components: a knowledge-tracing model estimates what a student knows, a recommender selects learning content, and a conversational tutor provides feedback. These components are not always coordinated as part of a single instructional decision process. Recent reviews of agentic and multi-agent AI in education show rapid growth in this area, but also point to a lack of longitudinal studies and carefully evaluated real-world deployments [3, 12]. To address this gap, we propose EduAgent-RL, a six-agent framework comprising Student Profiling, Learning Analytics, Content Recommendation, Assessment, Feedback, and Teacher/Supervisor agents. The agents are coordinated through centralized-training, decentralized-execution multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), supported by a knowledge-tracing state encoder, retrieval-grounded feedback, and an explicit human-oversight veto. The framework is evaluated on two public benchmarks, OULAD [14] and EdNet [2], against random, collaborative-filtering, classical machine-learning, single-agent RL, and RAG-based LLM tutor baselines. In the pilot evaluation, EduAgent-RL reached an AUROC of 0.83 and NDCG@10 of 0.71 on OULAD, compared with 0.74 AUROC / 0.58 NDCG@10 for the single-agent RL baseline and 0.79 AUROC / 0.63 NDCG@10 for the RAG-based tutor. The ablation results also showed the largest drop in performance when the knowledge-tracing encoder was removed.
radar.summary_short: Personalization in digital learning is often handled through separate components: a knowledge-tracing model estimates what a student knows, a recommender selects learning content, and a conversational tutor provides feedback.

radar.title: dITP shifts the assembly equilibrium of Kongming to activate NAD+ hydrolysis
radar.summary: Abstract The Kongming (Kom) system, consisting of KomA, KomB, and KomC, protects bacteria from phage infection. KomA collaborates with a phage enzyme to generate deoxyinosine 5′-triphosphate (dITP), which activates the KomBC complex to hydrolyze NAD⁺ and trigger cell death. Recent studies propose that dITP activates KomBC through a simple conformational change. Our findings instead reveal a more dynamic mechanism. Without dITP, KomBC complexes exist in equilibrium between tightly packed oligomers and loosely packed filaments, both inactive. Tight packing accumulates unfavorable electrostatic interactions without positioning catalytic residues for NAD⁺ hydrolysis, whereas loose packing relieves these interactions but leaves catalytic residues misaligned. dITP binding at KomB stabilizes tightly packed KomC cores in the filament while aligning catalytic residues. Therefore, a small-molecule signal activates signaling by shifting the assembly equilibrium of higher-order protein complexes toward a catalytically competent state.
radar.summary_short: Abstract The Kongming (Kom) system, consisting of KomA, KomB, and KomC, protects bacteria from phage infection. KomA collaborates with a phage enzyme to generate deoxyinosine 5′-triphosphate (dITP), which activates the KomBC complex to hydrolyze NAD⁺ and trigger cell death.

radar.title: TraceRouter++: Causal Semantic Routing Realignment via Optimal Transport
radar.venue_raw: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
radar.summary: Despite their remarkable capabilities, large foundation models (LFMs) remain susceptible to adversarial manipulation. Current safety intervention methods primarily rely on the locality hypothesis, rigidly suppressing isolated neurons or features. However, harmful semantics manifest as distributed, cross-layer circuits, rendering localized ablations both brittle against complex jailbreaks and detrimental to general utility. To bridge this gap, we propose TraceRouter++, a routing-level safety intervention framework that explicitly traces safety-relevant causal routing pathways activated under harmful inputs and realigns their unsafe activation states. Our framework operates in a Discover-Trace-Realign paradigm: it first pinpoints a sensitive onset layer via attention divergence and disentangles dense activations into interpretable routing features using sparse autoencoders (SAEs). Subsequently, it maps these features to downstream causal circuits via feature influence scores (FIS). Crucially, departing from rigid suppression paradigms, TraceRouter++ introduces a constrained optimal transport (OT)-based soft routing realignment. By formulating safety intervention as a tractable coordinate- wise marginal optimal transport approximation, our method redirects unsafe activation marginals toward safe-reference marginals within causally identified routing subspaces while preserving non-selected coordinates at the intervention point. This mechanism safely redirects malicious semantic flows while leaving orthogonal computational routes intact. Extensive experiments across representative large language models (LLMs), multimodal large language models (MLLMs), and diffusion models (DMs) show that TraceRouter++ outperforms evaluated baselines, improving adversarial robustness while maintaining a favorable safety-utility trade-off.
radar.summary_short: Despite their remarkable capabilities, large foundation models (LFMs) remain susceptible to adversarial manipulation. Current safety intervention methods primarily rely on the locality hypothesis, rigidly suppressing isolated neurons or features.

Recursive Adversarial Engine: A Stability-Oriented Architecture for Reliable Large Language Model Multi-Agent Systems
radar.venue: International Journal of Advanced AI Applications
radar.venue_raw: International Journal of Advanced AI Applications
radar.summary: Large language model (LLM) based multi-agent systems are rapidly migrating from laboratory prototypes to production deployments in finance, scientific research, industrial digital twins, and urban scheduling. As deployment scales, however, a family of systemic pathologies persists: decision oscillation driven by zero-sum agent interactions, cascade propagation of hallucinated content, long-horizon behavioral drift, value misalignment, and unresolved inter-agent conflict. Existing orchestration paradigms, which rely on instruction dispatch, greedy optimization, or static rules, address only shallow coordination and provide no principled mechanism for convergence. This paper proposes the Recursive Adversarial Engine (RAE), a runtime architecture for multi-agent systems organized around three propositions: bounded adversarial interaction supplies the error-detection signal, recursive correction supplies the error-elimination mechanism, and dynamic checks and balances supply the stability guarantee. We specify a four-layer reference architecture comprising adversarial verification, recursive correction, checks-and-balances scheduling, and steady-state output, and we characterize its convergence behavior through a Lyapunov-style stability argument. A qualitative comparison with self-play, multi-agent debate, alignment, and consensus frameworks delineates the paradigm difference. Engineering implications for high-stakes domains, long-horizon robustness, auditability, and middleware integration are analyzed, and open challenges are identified.
radar.summary_short: Large language model (LLM) based multi-agent systems are rapidly migrating from laboratory prototypes to production deployments in finance, scientific research, industrial digital twins, and urban scheduling.

radar.title: Certified Nash Equilibrium Learning for Nonzero-Sum Jump-Diffusion Games: Policy Iteration and Off-Policy Q-Learning
radar.summary: This paper establishes two model-free reinforcement learning methods for infinite-horizon N-player linear-quadratic nonzero-sum stochastic differential games whose drift, Brownian diffusion, and Poisson jump amplitudes depend on all players' controls. Control dependence in the diffusion and jump terms couples the players' simultaneous feedback updates. A verifiable certificate ensures that the partially model-free policy iteration map is contractive on an invariant closed ball centered at an admissible initial feedback profile. All feedback iterates are mean-square stabilizing, and the algorithm achieves local geometric convergence of feedback gains and value matrices to those associated with a closed-loop Nash equilibrium. The term certified refers to a verifiable convergence certificate that guarantees mean-square stability of all policy iterates and local geometric convergence to a closed-loop Nash equilibrium. To implement the policy updates from data, the off-policy Q-learning algorithm reuses the same behavior-policy data across iterations without requiring the system coefficients or jump intensity. Under quantitative persistence of excitation and a common initialization, exact population regression reproduces the policy-iteration sequence. The same local convergence guarantee therefore applies to off-policy Q-learning at the population level. Simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of the two proposed algorithms.
radar.summary_short: This paper establishes two model-free reinforcement learning methods for infinite-horizon N-player linear-quadratic nonzero-sum stochastic differential games whose drift, Brownian diffusion, and Poisson jump amplitudes depend on all players' controls.

radar.title: Public Signals in Affine Network Congestion Games with Uncertain Free-Flow Times
radar.summary: Travel times in road networks are subject to stochastic uncertainty resulting from various parameters. A benevolent mobility service provider observing the actual travel times from data may use its informational advantage to steer the traffic equilibrium in a favorable direction through a processs known as signaling or Bayesian persuasion. Previous work has shown that the underlying signaling problem can be NP-hard to approximate better than [Formula: see text], even for static Wardrop flows with affine cost functions with stochastic offsets. In contrast, we show that in this case, the signaling problem is easy for many networks. First, we tightly characterize the class of single-commodity networks in which full information revelation is always an optimal signaling strategy. Second, we construct a reduction from optimal signaling to computing an optimal collection of active edges for the Wardrop equilibrium. For two states, this allows us to efficiently compute an optimal signaling scheme whenever the number of different active edge sets is bounded by a polynomial in the input size. Using a cell decomposition technique, we extend the approach to a polynomial-time algorithm for multicommodity parallel-edge networks provided that both the number of commodities and states are constant. Funding: This work was supported by Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft EXC-2046/1 [Grant 390685689] and Ho 3831/9-1 [Grant 514505843].

radar.title: Strategic ignorance and information design
radar.summary: We study information design in strategic settings when agents can publicly refuse to view their private signals. Ignoring the constraints that agents must be willing to view their signals may lead to substantial divergence between the designer’s intent and actual outcomes, even in the case where the designer seeks to maximize the agents’ payoffs. We introduce the appropriate equilibrium concept — ignorance-permissive Bayes correlated equilibrium — and characterize implementable distributions over states and actions. The designer’s optimal response to strategic ignorance generates qualitative properties that standard information design cannot: the designer may provide redundant or even counterproductive information, asymmetric information structures may be strictly optimal in symmetric environments, providing information conditional on players’ viewing choices rather than all at once may hurt the designer, and communication between players may help her. Optimality sometimes requires that players ignore their signals with positive probability.

radar.title: Unified Human Motion Pretraining via Generative Chrono-Structural Decomposition and Alignment
radar.venue_raw: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
radar.summary: 3D human motion-language alignment remains challenging due to the complex entanglement of spatiotemporal semantics. Previous methods typically rely on holistic alignment, which overlooks fine-grained structural primitives, i.e., body parts and sub-events, inevitably leading to imprecise correspondences and limited generalization. To address this, we propose MoLA, a unified motion-language pretraining framework that explicitly decomposes and aligns motion/language at chronological and structural levels. Leveraging large language models (LLMs) as prior knowledge experts, we reformulate the coupled textual descriptions into structured part- and event-level motion concepts, enabling precise supervision for fine-grained alignment. Based on this, we further develop novel chrono-structural alignment mechanisms to facilitate correspondence learning. At the spatial level, we introduce a part-mixture learning strategy that decouples body-part motions to facilitate part-decorrelated correspondence modeling. At the temporal level, we propose Gumbel-based adaptive consistency learning coupled with a chronological order objective to address this weakly supervised event alignment task. This enables the model to dynamically localize relevant motion clips and learn temporally coherent correspondences without requiring explicit boundary annotations. Furthermore, a directional consistency regularization is involved that models semantic relationships between global motions and their local patterns. Extensive experiments on motion-text retrieval, recognition, captioning, and generation demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods, verifying our motivation and effectiveness for unified motion pretraining.

radar.title: Multiagent Assortment Optimization in Sequential Matching Markets
radar.summary: Motivated by the challenges faced by choice-based matching platforms, in this work, we study a generalization of the two-sided assortment optimization model. Specifically, this model consists of two sides (e.g., customers and suppliers) who have preferences over the opposite side in the form of discrete choice models. A matching is realized through a two-step process where the platform’s decision is to initially present to each agent on one side an assortment of users of the opposite side. The ultimate goal of the platform is to maximize the total expected revenue collected from the matching. Because of the computational complexity of this problem, we focus on the design of approximation algorithms with constant-factor guarantees for the constrained version of the problem under general choice preferences. First, to the best of our knowledge, we are the first to draw connections with the literature of submodular optimization and show that one-sided choice-oblivious approaches perform arbitrarily badly. Second, we show that, for the general setting, there exists a two-sided choice-aware randomized algorithm that achieves a [Formula: see text]-approximation factor, which is the best possible. Third, we design an algorithm that is asymptotically optimal when one side follows the well-known multinomial logit (MNL) choice model under the small probability regime. Fourth, we provide a simple and effective algorithm with a [Formula: see text]-approximation guarantee for the unconstrained setting, with both sides following MNL models. Finally, we assess the performance of our proposed methods with a detailed computational study and discuss several extensions. Funding: M. radar.title: Multi-AI agent framework reveals the “oxide gatekeeper” in aluminum nanoparticle oxidation
radar.venue_raw: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
radar.summary: Aluminum nanoparticles (ANPs) are among the most energy-dense solid fuels, yet the atomic mechanisms governing their transition from passivated particles to highly reactive states remain elusive. This stems from a fundamental computational bottleneck: Ab initio methods offer quantum-level fidelity but are restricted to small spatiotemporal scales (<500 atoms, picoseconds), while empirical force fields lack the reactive fidelity required for complex combustion environments. Here, we bridge this gap by employing a human-audited, multiagent framework to make the development and validation of a task-specific machine learning potential (MLP) more traceable and auditable. The workflow coordinates active learning, model evaluation, validation evidence, and human expert review, while leaving scientific interpretation and model-use decisions under researcher control. This collaborative cycle ensures quantum mechanical accuracy while exhibiting near-linear scalability. Strikingly, our simulations reveal a temperature-regulated dual-mode oxidation mechanism: At moderate temperatures, the oxide shell acts as a dynamic “gatekeeper,” regulating oxidation through a “breathing mode” of transient nanochannels; above a critical threshold, a “rupture mode” leads to shell failure and rapid combustion. Importantly, we resolve a decades-old controversy by demonstrating that aluminum cation outward diffusion, rather than oxygen transport, dominates mass transfer in studied regimes, with diffusion coefficients consistently exceeding those of oxygen by 2 to 3 orders of magnitude. These results provide an atomistic framework for interpreting ANP reactivity and illustrate how human-audited agentic workflows can make domain-specific reactive MLP development and deployment more reproducible.
radar.summary_short: Aluminum nanoparticles (ANPs) are among the most energy-dense solid fuels, yet the atomic mechanisms governing their transition from passivated particles to highly reactive states remain elusive.

radar.title: Reframing decentralized diagnostics with a programmable multi-dimensional microfluidic system
Implementation via political parties
radar.summary: We address the implementation of public policies (alternatives) when the feasible set is unknown to the planner. The implementing agents are the political parties, who know the feasible set. They care about the implemented alternative, which reflects their ideology, and their share in parliament and office. They face a mechanism that, given the alternatives proposed by all parties, asks the voters to rank them and determines the chosen alternative and the shares in parliament and office. We identify conditions on parties’ preferences that guarantee the socially optimal policy is the outcome of the unique pure strategy Nash equilibrium of the electoral game played by the parties. The existence of the equilibrium does not require any assumptions about the parties’ ideology. To ensure uniqueness, shares must prevail over ideology: office or parliamentary shares in two-party systems, and strictly office shares in systems with more than two parties.
radar.summary_short: We address the implementation of public policies (alternatives) when the feasible set is unknown to the planner. The implementing agents are the political parties, who know the feasible set.

radar.title: TRUE: Towards Robust, Unique, and Efficient Model Fingerprint Generation and Verification
radar.venue_raw: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
radar.summary: While deep neural networks (DNNs) are being widely adopted, they are also increasingly exposed to model stealing risks, posing significant threats to intellectual property. Model fingerprinting, which utilizes intrinsic characteristics derived from the training process to authenticate models, has been proposed as a potential solution. An ideal fingerprint should satisfy robustness, uniqueness, and efficiency. However, existing methods often struggle to balance these three aspects simultaneously. To address this challenge, we propose TRUE, a twostage fingerprint generation and verification framework. In the fingerprint generation stage, we adopt adversarial examples as the fingerprint type and enhance their robustness through a minmax robust optimization strategy. In the fingerprint verification stage, we assign weights to the adversarial examples using a Boltzmann distribution to reflect their uniqueness, and further employ sampling based on these weights to reduce the number of queries and improve efficiency. Extensive experiments conducted on real-world datasets and across different model architectures demonstrate the superiority of the TRUE framework.

radar.title: Towards Robust Multi-View Clustering via Early-to-late Manifold Consistency Calibration
radar.venue_raw: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
radar.summary: For multi-view data, structural heterogeneity across views is a common property, with cross-view sparsity variation serving as a typical manifestation. To first account for this sparsity-induced heterogeneity, we develop Adaptive View-specific Encoding, which incorporates the sparsity ratio of each view as prior knowledge for view-aware representation learning and constraint modulation. Based thereon, we further tackle the broader issue of view quality imbalance in multi-view fusion, where low-quality views introduce unreliable structural relations and view-specific constraints further amplify latent discrepancies. To this end, we propose a globallocal manifold-guided fusion mechanism named Early-to-late Manifold Consistency Calibration, which leverages the relatively stable global manifold preserved in early-fused encoded features to modulate robust late-stage fusion of adaptively encoded local features. Specifically, the early-stage global features serve as a structural anchor for assessing the manifold consistency of features of each adaptively encoded local view. The resulting consistency scores are then used to adaptively reweight late-stage global fusion, attenuating structurally unreliable views while reinforcing those aligned with the common manifold. In this manner, latent manifold consistency enables early fusion to calibrate late-stage fusion, thereby establishing a principled connection between adaptive view-specific encoding and cross-view distribution alignment. The full framework, named Manifold Consistency Guided Adaptive Sparse Autoencoder for Multiview Clustering (MASA), is validated on multiple datasets and demonstrates superior effectiveness and robustness across diverse experimental settings. On ALOI-100, MASA further enhances clustering stability, reducing the fluctuation standard deviation over the final rounds from 3.02% to 1.28%.

radar.title: CoopDistill: Equilibrium-Guided Multi-Agent Policy Distillation for Cooperative Driving
radar.summary: Cooperative driving extends autonomous driving from individual vehicle decisions to joint maneuvers that improve traffic safety and efficiency. Optimization-based methods impose safety constraints but often fix paths to simplify multi-vehicle planning, limiting spatial flexibility. Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) explores alternatives through interaction, but coordinated learning and safe execution remain challenging. Their integration nevertheless faces challenges in exploration efficiency, experience allocation, and execution reliability. To address these challenges, this paper proposes CoopDistill, an equilibrium-guided multi-agent policy distillation framework. A potential-game (PG) formulation provides a fixed-path longitudinal reference, around which a residual MARL policy learns longitudinal acceleration, conflict-approach timing, and lateral path corrections. A hard-case curriculum concentrates experience on interactions that PG leaves unresolved or substantially delayed. A comparative rollout selector evaluates the joint consequences of learned corrections against PG before choosing the executed action. Experiments in merging, roundabout, and intersection scenarios compare CoopDistill with six baselines at four connected automated vehicle penetration levels. Relative to PG, success improves by 2.1--27.1 percentage points and delay decreases by 7.3--27.3\%, with no observed collisions. Code is available at https://github.com/FanGShiYuu/CoopDistill
radar.summary_short: Cooperative driving extends autonomous driving from individual vehicle decisions to joint maneuvers that improve traffic safety and efficiency. Optimization-based methods impose safety constraints but often fix paths to simplify multi-vehicle planning, limiting spatial flexibility.

radar.title: Autonomous biomedical research with an artificial intelligence agent
radar.summary: Biomedical research is increasingly constrained by repetitive, fragmented workflows that slow discovery. We introduce Biomni, a general-purpose biomedical artificial intelligence agent that autonomously executes diverse research tasks. To map the biomedical action space, Biomni’s action-discovery agent mines tools, databases, and protocols from thousands of publications across 25 domains, building a unified agentic environment. Its general-purpose architecture integrates large language model reasoning with retrieval-augmented planning and code-based execution, dynamically composing workflows without predefined templates. Systematic benchmarking shows strong generalization across heterogeneous tasks—causal gene prioritization, drug repurposing, rare-disease diagnosis, microbiome analysis, and molecular cloning—without task-specific tuning. Real-world case studies demonstrate Biomni interpreting multimodal datasets, optimizing protein stability, orchestrating wet-lab instruments, and generating experimentally testable protocols. Biomni envisions artificial intelligence augmenting human scientists and accelerating discovery.
radar.summary_short: Biomedical research is increasingly constrained by repetitive, fragmented workflows that slow discovery. We introduce Biomni, a general-purpose biomedical artificial intelligence agent that autonomously executes diverse research tasks.

radar.title: Q-Eval+: From Absolute to Relative Quality Evaluation for Text-to-Vision Content
radar.venue_raw: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
radar.summary: Text-to-vision (T2V) models are rapidly reshaping content creation, yet their outputs still require careful human screening before deployment in real applications. This creates an urgent need for evaluation tools that can 1) assign reliable absolute quality scores and 2) support fine-grained relative comparisons for model selection, reranking, and online A/B testing. Existing T2V benchmarks, however, are often limited by entangled definitions of visual quality and text-vision alignment, narrow coverage of images or videos, and the absence of systematically constructed pairwise and diagnostic annotations. Therefore, we present Q-Eval+, a large-scale dataset to jointly support absolute scoring and relative comparing for T2V content. Q-Eval+ consists of 220K image/video instances with 1.32M human annotations along two key dimensions: Q-Eval-Abs provides MOS-style labels for visual quality and alignment at both instance and model levels, while Q-Eval-Rel offers side-by-side preferences and choice-based VQA questions that reveal not only which instance is better, but also why. On top of Q-Eval+, we develop Q-Evaluator, a unified large multimodal model that bridges absolute and relative assessment through supervised fine-tuning with structured context prompts and a Vague-to-Specific alignment handling strategy. We further introduce symmetric and consistency accuracies to evaluate robustness under pairwise permutations. Extensive experiments show that Q-Evaluator achieves consistently strong correlations with human opinions and competitive comparative accuracy against existing open-source and proprietary LMM-based evaluators, providing a practical foundation for robust T2V quality control.

radar.title: Invariance, Stability, and Diversity: A Unified Framework for Multimodal Domain Generalization
radar.venue_raw: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
radar.summary: Multimodal Domain Generalization (MMDG) aims to learn models that generalize to unseen domains under unpredictable, modality-dependent distribution shifts. Despite recent progress, existing methods often rely on heuristic fusion strategies and lack a unified theoretical perspective, limiting their robustness under domain shifts. In this paper, we identify three fundamental challenges in MMDG: (I) insufficient cross-domain invariance across individual modalities and cross-modal interaction subspaces; (II) instability induced by asynchronous modality degradation, through which unreliable modalities impair joint representations; and (III) limited representation diversity, which exacerbates source-target support mismatch. To characterize these challenges, we derive a generalization error bound for a stability-weighted ensemble of modality-wise hypotheses, revealing three corresponding factors: Invariance (Source-Source Divergence), Stability (Stability-Weighted Error), and Diversity (Target-Convex Hull Divergence). Guided by this analysis, we develop a unified nonlinear fusion framework comprising Multi-Granularity Adversarial Alignment to promote invariance across modality-specific, interaction, and fusion spaces, Stability-Aware Adaptive Learning to prioritize reliable modalities during source training and mitigate asynchronous degradation, and Manifold Expansion to increase normalized source-feature dispersion as a source-side regularizer. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks show that our framework achieves the best overall average rank across 43 transfer tasks on seven datasets spanning four task families and eight diverse modalities.

radar.title: Infrastructure-Based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Attention for Highway Ramp Merging
radar.summary: On-ramp merging is a typical safety and throughput problem on highways. Without proper coordination, human drivers and self-interested autonomous vehicles may make risky manoeuvres and cause accidents or congestion. With recent advances in connected autonomous vehicles (CAVs) and multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), vehicles can be trained to coordinate for safe and efficient merging. However, in dense traffic, forming an effective observation of the traffic state is challenging. For example, observing only the neighbouring vehicles may lead to locally optimal decisions, while observing the entire traffic can introduce much irrelevant information. In this paper, we propose a transformer-based MARL vehicle control model to address these problems. A roadside infrastructure controller receives the states of all CAVs via vehicle-to-infrastructure (V2I) communication and sends control commands back to them. An attention-based observation encoder is designed where each vehicle can filter the relevant vehicle information from the global traffic state. The proposed model is evaluated in SUMO against three baselines: a model that observes only the neighbouring vehicles, a model that encodes the global traffic information, and the rule-based SUMO model. The results show that our model achieves the highest traffic flow, safety and smoothness. Furthermore, in a four-hour simulation with dynamic traffic demand, our model successfully avoids traffic jams, while other baseline models fail at high traffic flow. We also show that our model remains effective when human-driven vehicles are present. We further show that our model, trained in ideal communication conditions, can still remain collision-free and maintain throughput under realistic V2I communication errors. Finally, we visualise the relevance weights that an ego vehicle assigns to other vehicles in multiple traffic situations.
radar.summary_short: On-ramp merging is a typical safety and throughput problem on highways. Without proper coordination, human drivers and self-interested autonomous vehicles may make risky manoeuvres and cause accidents or congestion.

radar.title: Evaluating Authorization and Trust Boundaries in Agentic Orchestration Frameworks
radar.summary: Agentic AI systems extend large language models with tools, memory, and multi-agent collaboration, introducing security risks at orchestration boundaries. These risks depend on how identities are represented, operations are authorized, and instructions or information propagate between components. We evaluate LangChain, LangGraph, AutoGen, and OpenClaw through twelve experiments mapped to the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications using a common LLM (gpt-4o-mini). The experiments cover prompt injection, unauthorized resource access and command execution, memory poisoning, and inter-agent trust and identity attacks. Adversarial inputs induced unauthorized tool invocation, while tool chaining, stale filesystem validation, encoded instructions, and inter-agent delegation exposed weaknesses in authorization across component boundaries. Memory poisoning showed that untrusted state can influence responses, a risk distinct from conventional access-control violations. In the evaluated protected configurations, explicit authorization, controlled capability assignment, filesystem containment, and execution safeguards prevented specific unauthorized operations. The findings emphasize preserving authorization and information-trust boundaries throughout agentic workflows rather than treating framework capabilities or model-level instructions as sufficient security guarantees.
radar.summary_short: Agentic AI systems extend large language models with tools, memory, and multi-agent collaboration, introducing security risks at orchestration boundaries. These risks depend on how identities are represented, operations are authorized, and instructions or information propagate between components.

radar.title: Preserved higher-order mentalising during strategic interactions after medial prefrontal cortex damage
radar.summary: Abstract Mentalising, the ability to infer the beliefs and intentions of others, is essential for successful social interaction. Previous studies have implicated the medial prefrontal cortex in mentalising, but whether this region is necessary for higher-order mentalising remains unclear. Here we show that people with focal damage to the medial prefrontal cortex retain the ability to engage in higher-order mentalising during a strategic social game. We compare their performance with patients with brain damage in other regions and lesion-free participants. Individuals with medial prefrontal cortex damage achieve similar rewards and use comparable mentalising strategies, but they are slower when making strategic decisions. Computational modelling indicates that this slowing reflects a greater tendency to require evidence before committing to a choice. Voxel-based lesion-symptom mapping identifies medial prefrontal regions linked to altered decision processes rather than mentalising. These findings suggest that the medial prefrontal cortex supports strategic decisions while higher-order mentalising remains intact.
radar.summary_short: Abstract Mentalising, the ability to infer the beliefs and intentions of others, is essential for successful social interaction. Previous studies have implicated the medial prefrontal cortex in mentalising, but whether this region is necessary for higher-order mentalising remains unclear.

radar.title: Multitype Information Acquisition in a Strategic Trading Model
radar.summary: We analyze information acquisition in a strategic trading model with multidimensional uncertainties. Our main result is that the equilibrium can exhibit multiplicity because of the integer nature of the number of informed traders and the strategic interactions across different types of informed traders. We show that the number of equilibria can be arbitrarily large. Moreover, asymmetric equilibria can arise even in symmetric settings. As information costs rise, fewer traders acquire information, yet prices can become more informative. These results shed light on the instability of financial markets and yield testable empirical predictions. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. radar.title: Contest or Contract: Assessing the Effectiveness of Contests in Online Labor Markets
radar.summary: Online labor markets have become increasingly popular among companies seeking global access to workers. Some platforms have adopted a contest-based scheme, allowing employers to review multiple submissions before selecting the best one. This practice raises a crucial question: Given a predefined budget, should employers choose a contest or contract scheme for tasks? This study examines the comparative effectiveness of contests versus contracts in achieving better job outcomes, focusing on design tasks characterized by high uncertainty. Using a comprehensive data set from a leading online labor market, we employ multiple empirical strategies, combined with machine learning and text mining techniques, to examine the impact of compensation schemes on job quality. Our results suggest that contract-based jobs yield better performance than contests in the context of ideation tasks. Further analysis, such as examining image similarity among pairwise solutions within a task, identifies “copying” behaviors as a key mechanism undermining the effectiveness of contests. In the public setting of contests, workers can observe others’ submissions and revise their own, leading to imitation rather than innovation. As competition intensity increases, workers have weaker incentives to exert effort, reducing solution quality. Consequently, the negative incentive effects in contests outweigh both the potential positive incentive and parallel effects. Moreover, although information availability can enhance work quality, contests inherently offer limited informational advantages compared with contracts. Taken together, our findings suggest that contract-based schemes are more effective than contests for design tasks, offering important implications for both employers and platform designers in online labor markets. This paper was accepted by Karan Girotra, operations management. Funding: N. Zhang acknowledges the support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72302053]. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07082 .
radar.summary_short: Online labor markets have become increasingly popular among companies seeking global access to workers. Some platforms have adopted a contest-based scheme, allowing employers to review multiple submissions before selecting the best one.

radar.title: Nash Equilibrium-Driven Adaptive Behavior in Swarm Intelligence with Self-Organizing Maps
radar.summary: This paper proposes a swarm intelligence model that employs classical boid flocking dynamics combined with non-cooperative game-theoretic methods, specifically Nash Equilibrium, to simulate adaptive decision-making in multi-agent systems. The work leverages a payoff matrix based on fundamental flocking behaviors: cohesion, alignment, and separation, to enable each agent to dynamically optimize its own strategy based on local interactions within the group. The simulation introduces Self-Organizing Maps (SOMs) for clustering and behavior adaptation, providing a machine learning perspective on agent categorization and role differentiation. To simulate real-world unpredictability, stochastic noise is used to understand how varying noise levels influence collective alignment and coherence. The results demonstrate the impact of environmental factors on emergent swarm behavior and showcase the benefits of combining machine learning and game theory for adaptive control in distributed systems. This work provides valuable insights into the interplay between noise, decision-making, and flocking dynamics, with broader applications in robotics, swarm intelligence, and autonomous systems.
radar.summary_short: This paper proposes a swarm intelligence model that employs classical boid flocking dynamics combined with non-cooperative game-theoretic methods, specifically Nash Equilibrium, to simulate adaptive decision-making in multi-agent systems.

radar.title: Game theory driven multi-agent framework mitigates language model hallucination
On the Maximization of Long-Run Conditional Value-at-Risk for Markov Decision Processes
radar.summary: Optimizing Risk-Seeking Sequential Decisions via Conditional Value-at-Risk Decision makers may exhibit risk-seeking preferences in finance, energy operations, and stochastic resource management, yet corresponding Markov decision process (MDP) theories remain underdeveloped. In this paper, “On the Maximization of Long-Run CVaR for Markov Decision Processes,” Xia, Yu, and Wu investigate infinite-horizon MDPs maximizing long-run conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) for instantaneous rewards. They prove optimality for stationary randomized policies and show deterministic policies may fail; an optimal policy randomizes over at most two actions. By converting the original problem into a minimax saddle point formulation, the authors develop solvable linear programming and globally convergent gradient descent algorithms. Results are further extended to joint mean-CVaR optimization and validated on real-world microgrid scheduling data. This work fills gaps for risk-seeking MDPs and delivers practical computation tools for tail-oriented sequential decision making.
radar.summary_short: Optimizing Risk-Seeking Sequential Decisions via Conditional Value-at-Risk Decision makers may exhibit risk-seeking preferences in finance, energy operations, and stochastic resource management, yet corresponding Markov decision process (MDP) theories remain underdeveloped.

radar.title: Multi-Agent Cooperative Decision-Making for Connected and Automated Vehicles: A Survey of Methods, Scenarios, and Deployment Challenges
radar.summary: Connected and Automated Vehicles (CAVs) are expected to improve road safety and traffic efficiency, but achieving this remains challenging. This paper presents a methodologically organized survey of cooperative decision-making approaches for CAV systems, tracing their chronological development within each methodological family. The literature is categorized into rule-based and control-theoretic methods; game-theoretic models; single-agent and multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) approaches; and large language model (LLM)-, vision language model (VLM)-, multimodal large language model (MLLM)-, and foundation-model-based decision support. The reviewed studies address a range of traffic scenarios, including platooning, lane changes, merging, intersections, traffic signals, and mixed-traffic environments. The review compares these methods based on safety, scalability, communication requirements, interpretability, sim-to-real transfer, and mixed-traffic performance. The selected literature illustrates MARL-based approaches to cooperative CAV decision-making; its composition is not used to infer publication growth or the prevalence of methods across the field. Nevertheless, the reviewed MARL methods face challenges concerning safety, communication, scalability, interpretability, and transfer from simulation to real-world deployment. Overall, no single method addresses all the requirements of cooperative CAV systems. Hybrid architectures combining MARL with complementary methods are therefore a promising direction for future CAV systems.

radar.title: RAD-2: Scaling Reinforcement Learning in a Generator-Discriminator Framework
radar.venue_raw: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
radar.summary: High-level autonomous driving requires motion planners capable of modeling multimodal future uncertainties while remaining robust in closed-loop interactions. Although diffusion-based planners are effective at modeling complex trajectory distributions, they often suffer from stochastic instabilities and the lack of corrective negative feedback when trained purely with imitation learning. To address these issues, we propose RAD-2, a unified generator-discriminator framework for closed-loop planning. Specifically, a diffusion-based generator is used to produce diverse trajectory candidates, while an RL-optimized discriminator reranks these candidates according to their long-term driving quality. This decoupled design avoids directly applying sparse scalar rewards to the full high-dimensional trajectory space, thereby improving optimization stability. To further enhance reinforcement learning, we introduce Temporally Consistent Group Relative Policy Optimization, which exploits temporal coherence to alleviate the credit assignment problem. In addition, we propose On-policy Generator Optimization, which converts closed-loop feedback into structured longitudinal optimization signals and progressively shifts the generator toward high-reward trajectory manifolds. To support efficient large-scale training, we introduce BEV-Warp, a high- throughput simulation environment that performs closed-loop evaluation directly in Bird's-Eye View feature space via spatial warping. RAD-2 reduces the collision rate by 56% compared with strong diffusion-based planners. Preliminary real-world mainpaper validation on four routes across two cities further indicates improved perceived safety and driving smoothness in complex urban traffic. Videos of closed-loop simulations, real-world deployments, and comparative experiments are available at https://hgao-cv.github.io/RAD-2.
radar.summary_short: High-level autonomous driving requires motion planners capable of modeling multimodal future uncertainties while remaining robust in closed-loop interactions. radar.title: Macro Control and Capability Evaluation of Black-Box World Models: A Two-Regime Framework for LLM-Agent Markets
radar.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents can be organized into multi-agent markets that act as world models, mapping macro information to emergent macro dynamics while the evaluator observes only macro inputs and outputs. This paper separates a model's capability into two stages that a single aggregate score cannot separate: information simulation, from macro information to micro behavior, and macro emergence, from micro behavior to the macro outcome. We introduce a soft macro-control method that announces a public reference path day by day without touching individual decisions, orders, or matching, and a two-regime evaluation framework that measures both stages from macro observations alone. In the reference-only regime the symmetric true and flipped references share a common level R, which measures realization under the announced reference, while their paired gap B measures structural bias; in the information-injection regime external information dilutes the reference, so only the true-flipped gap Delta remains interpretable. On five single-index LLM-agent markets, announcing a target path shifts the realized path toward the announced target on both announced references under both information conditions. Relative to the no-reference path, the tracking score is higher by 0.306 and 0.415 without news and by 0.183 and 0.329 with news; within the stock/cash scan structural bias is lowest at 70/30 (B=0.042); realization peaks at a 3:7 technical share (R=0.894 versus 0.358 for technical-only); and Delta is 0.0341 with fundamental data and 0.0487 with news. Both stages use the same two observable scores, each read in the regime where it is interpretable.
radar.summary_short: Large language model (LLM) agents can be organized into multi-agent markets that act as world models, mapping macro information to emergent macro dynamics while the evaluator observes only macro inputs and outputs.

radar.title: Bargaining and Contract Forms in Distribution Channels: Why Do Slotting Fees Arise and Linear Contracts Persist?
radar.summary: Two empirical patterns emerge in business-to-business settings, particularly in retail distribution channels such as grocery markets. First, linear contracts are widely observed alongside nonlinear contracts with fixed payments, despite the claimed efficiency advantages of the latter. Second, when fixed payments arise, they often flow from suppliers to retailers (slotting fees) rather than the reverse. We develop and analyze a model of multilateral bargaining in which a supplier negotiates separately with competing retailers to explain these patterns. The key mechanism is a trade-off between two distortions: under linear contracts, wholesale prices reflect bargaining power and can be either above or below the channel-profit-maximizing level, whereas under two-part tariffs, wholesale prices are set to maximize bilateral surplus independently of bargaining power but are systematically too low from an overall channel perspective because of rent shifting across relationships. As a result, neither contractual form uniformly dominates; instead, relative performance depends on how bargaining shapes gains from trade across firms. When bargaining leads to slotting fees, two-part tariffs yield higher channel profits than linear contracts, whereas when it would imply payments from retailers to suppliers, linear contracts may perform better. These findings offer a unified explanation for the persistence of linear contracts alongside two-part tariffs, the direction of fixed payments, and the conditions under which each contractual form is likely to arise. This paper was accepted by Miguel Villas-Boas, marketing. Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.03426 .
radar.summary_short: Two empirical patterns emerge in business-to-business settings, particularly in retail distribution channels such as grocery markets. First, linear contracts are widely observed alongside nonlinear contracts with fixed payments, despite the claimed efficiency advantages of the latter.

radar.title: Optional Traps: An Empirical Study of LLM Agents Against Credential Deception and Alert-Driven Revocation
radar.summary: Deception (honeypots, decoys and canary credentials) rests on a simple premise: legitimate users never touch a fake asset, so any touch is a high-confidence signal. We ask whether that premise holds when the attacker is a large language model (LLM) agent, and what deception contributes once ordinary hardening is in place. We built an isolated, hash-chained lab around a mock Records API and report four studies. (1) In an exploratory run, a local 9.7B-parameter model ignored every optional decoy, read a genuinely leaked service key from a debug endpoint and exported the protected records in both static and adaptive deception modes. (2) After removing the leak, planting a canary credential in its place and revoking the offending client, a frozen 60-session study with a 4B-parameter model found export success of 20/20 at baseline, 0/20 with hardening alone and 0/20 with hardening plus deception (exact paired McNemar p = 1.9e-6 baseline vs. defended; p = 1 hardened vs. defended). Deception added detection and per-client revocation in 19 of 20 defended sessions, but no measurable prevention beyond hardening. (3) On Google Cloud, a real OpenCanary login alert was authenticated, signed and turned into revocation of the attacking client; the first denied export followed within an observed upper bound of 303 ms, a separate legitimate client completed 100/100 requests, and all 14 control checks passed. (4) In multi-agent swarm engagements, agents that used the canary were revoked 39-59 s after the bait was served without affecting siblings, but one model-driven legitimate agent also took the bait, a false-positive risk specific to LLM clients. Against LLM agents, traps must sit on the attacker's path rather than beside it, closing real weaknesses does the preventive work, and deception's measurable value is fast, attributable detection. All results are lab-scale and are not a production claim.

radar.title: Approximation and Error Bounds for Zero-Sum Stopping Games with Probability Criteria
radar.summary: This paper studies a two-person zero-sum stochastic game, which must terminate when either player quits the game or a state of the game first enters a prescribed target set. The performance criterion is the probability that the total reward reaches a given threshold. First, under a mild condition, we prove the existence of the value and a Nash equilibrium of the game by developing a comparison theorem. Second, for solving the game with infinite states, we develop a finite-state approximation method based on truncation, and derive explicit error bounds between the values of the truncated and original games. Third, using the error bounds, we design an effective algorithm, by which we can not only obtain any approximation of the value and Nash equilibria of the original game, but also provide convergence analysis of the approximation. Finally, a queueing example is used to illustrate the advantage of our condition and the effectiveness of our algorithm.
